schools.summary: Gill derives 'wild goats of the rock' from their rock-dwelling habit, and grounds their unknown birth-time in the inaccessibility of the crags where (per Olympiodorus) they bring forth.

Clarke gives the philology (yael, 'to ascend') and insists the question turns on the circumstances of providence, not the bare time: the herb seselis and thunder easing the hind's delivery (Ps. 29:9).
Henry makes the panel a proof of providence preserving every species, and turns the hind's aided calving into comfort for women in labour.

Keil and Delitzsch render the strophe of the ibices and stags, deriving yelim from a root 'to mount' and reading the infinitive of bringing forth with pangs, with notes on the plene spelling and euphonic endings.
Gill tallies the naturalists' gestation figures (goats five months per Pliny, hinds eight) and confesses the wild goats' term is nowhere recorded.
Henry: man is wholly ignorant of the time they bring forth, unable to count the months of a wild goat's pregnancy.
Gill reads 'they bow themselves' of the birthing crouch, aided by thunder and the herbs seselis (before) and aros (after) to ease the hinds' hard labour.
Clarke takes 'sorrows' (chebleyhem) not of the pangs but of the afterbirth, the placenta or umbilical cord cast out with the young.
Keil and Delitzsch render the three strokes: they bow down, let their young break through, cast off their pains.
Henry: their sorrows are cast out and forgotten by good providence, and (per Ps. 29:9) God helps even the hinds to calve — comfort for women in labour.

debates.question: What does 'they cast out their sorrows' (chebleyhem) mean?

sides.position: the birth-pangs, thrown off as the young are freed
the afterbirth — the placenta or umbilical cord

schools.summary: Clarke (with Houbigant and Good) reads bar as 'open field' not corn and the young as growing independent and returning no more; Wesley keeps 'as with corn' and grounds their going forth in providence.
Ellicott prefers 'in the open field'; Keil and Delitzsch render 'grow up in the desert, run away and do not return.'
Gill reads the young as plump and sleek fawns, 'in good liking,' thriving without man's help.
Henry makes the weaned fawns an example to children — to put forth themselves and not always hang upon their parents.

debates.question: Does 'grow up with corn' (bar) mean fed as with grain, or grown in the open field?

sides.position: as with corn — fed as if with grain
in the open field / the desert

schools.summary: Gill hears the whole riddle in 'free': the wild ass is naturally averse to servitude, and only God gave it that nature, longing, and power to keep its liberty.
Clarke identifies the pere/onager (distinct from the zebra) and notes the parallel arod, the 'brayer'; Wesley reduces the clauses to 'who gave him this love of freedom and keeps him from the bands?'
Henry weighs the liberty and finds it a doubtful prize — better to labour and be good for something than to ramble and be good for nothing.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the barren land his dwellings' and note the Hebrew pointing (dagesh, retreating accent).
Gill: God appointed the wilderness the wild ass's house, fitted to its nature and safe from subjection (Arabia's deserts, per Xenophon and Leo Africanus).
Clarke fixes 'the barren land' as melechah, the salt land or salt places.
Henry turns the unenclosed lodging into a parable: the wild ass snuffs the wind (Jer. 2:24) but must house its liberty in a barren land — he that will not labour, let him not eat.
Gill: the wild ass scorns the crowd that would take it, outrunning all but the Barbary horse (Xenophon, Leo Africanus); or reads 'the noise of the city.'
Clarke: so swift it cannot be hunted down; Wesley: it fears not its pursuers and will not receive the driver's yoke.
Ellicott renders 'the shoutings of the taskmaster,' the word being that used of Egypt's taskmasters, and asks whether a reminiscence of the bondage is intended.
Henry: having no owner, the wild ass is in no subjection, and laughs (per Bishop Patrick) at those who live in the tumult of cities.

outliers.note: Suggests 'the crying of the driver' uses the very word for Egypt's taskmasters, hinting at a possible reminiscence of the Egyptian bondage in the free desert creature.

schools.summary: Gill: the wild ass ranges and searches the mountains for its short commons, a bare pasture.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing.'
Clarke: the mountains and desert are his pasture, living on anything green; Wesley: he prefers that mean provision with freedom before the fattest pastures with servitude.
Henry: with no feeder he must shift for himself — and from the untameable creature we learn how unfit we are to give law to Providence, who cannot give law to a wild ass's colt.

themes: the unfitness to give law to God

schools.summary: Clarke gives up the fabled one-horned unicorn to the heralds and identifies reem firmly as the rhinoceros; Wesley records the dispute (rhinoceros or wild bull) without deciding.
Ellicott rejects the rhinoceros for the buffalo/wild ox (cf. the domestic-ox contrast, Ps. 22:21); Keil and Delitzsch render the word 'oryx.'
Gill treats the fabled unicorn's very existence as doubtful, listing the 'monocerots,' and holds the Scripture creature must be one strong and well known to Job.
Henry takes reem for a strong, stately wild bull (Num. 23:22), able to serve but not willing, whom God challenges Job to force to the crib.

sides.position: the buffalo, wild ox, or oryx
uncertain / the name left in doubt

themes: a strength that will not serve

schools.summary: Gill spells out the impossible husbandry — yoke, harness, and plough on the wild ox: thou canst not.
Keil and Delitzsch render (of the 'oryx') the leading-rein in the furrow and the harrowed valleys, setting the comedy in its strophe.
Henry reads the beast's refusal as an effect of sin: man having revolted from his Maker is justly punished by the revolt of the creatures from him, yet some are still serviceable.

themes: the wild ox at the plough

schools.summary: Gill contrasts the manageable tame ox with the wild ox — stronger, fitter, yet not to be trusted, unruly (Caesar's untameable uri).
Keil and Delitzsch render 'wilt thou trust him because his strength is great, and leave thy labour to him?'
Henry: a disposition to labour is as much God's gift as the ability; a great mercy when, where God gives strength, he gives a heart to serve.

themes: trust the tame ox not the wild
the heart to labour as God's gift

schools.summary: Gill: thou knowest him too well to believe he will bring the sheaves home in safety.
Ellicott glosses 'believe' as 'trust/feel confidence in him'; Keil and Delitzsch render bringing in the sowing and garnering the threshing-floor.
Clarke: no domestic or agricultural use can be made of him.
Henry: because he will not serve about the corn he is not fed like the tame ox; his Maker never designed him for it.

themes: the barn the wild ox never darkens

schools.summary: Clarke would render renanim 'ostriches,' chasidah 'stork,' notsah 'hawk/pelican,' and (with Good) contrasts the ostrich's flapping wing with the stork's and falcon's flight; her vibration gives unrivalled running speed.
Ellicott renders 'the wing of the ostrich is superb, but are her pinions like the stork's?'; Keil and Delitzsch: 'the wing of the ostrich vibrates joyously; is she pious, wing and feather?'
Gill reads 'ostriches' not peacocks (whose glory is the tail), doubting the peacock was even known in Job's time.
Henry alone keeps the peacock in view beside the ostrich, reading the common point of proud, goodly feathers — beauty without wisdom.

debates.question: Is the bird of the verse the peacock or the ostrich (and is chasidah the ostrich or the stork)?

sides.position: the ostrich, not the peacock (Clarke and Ellicott further make chasidah the stork)
the peacock kept in view alongside the ostrich

themes: the wing that runs but cannot fly

schools.summary: Clarke gathers the travellers (Jackson, Shaw): the ostrich lays thirty to fifty eggs in the sand, forsakes them, and reserves most for food.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'warmeth them in dust'; Ellicott notes she sits only by night, the sand hatching them by day.
Gill cites Aelianus and Leo Africanus on the low sand-nest and the ten or twelve cannon-ball eggs.
Henry: unlike the nesting sparrow (Ps. 84:3), the ostrich is a 'monster in nature,' dropping her eggs anywhere and refusing to warm them.
Gill: the traveller's foot may crush the eggs unawares, and the creature has no foresight to prevent it.
Keil and Delitzsch render the twofold peril — the foot may crush, the wild beast may break them.
Clarke finds the travellers' reports confirming the text to the letter, the poet exactly acquainted with his subject.
Henry asks how the species survives, answering by providence: God hatches the neglected eggs (as he feeds the young ravens), or she does not always leave them.
Gill, citing Aelianus, softens the charge: the ostrich is tender to the young she hatches, and hardened only through forgetfulness against the true young she has muddled and lost.
Keil and Delitzsch render the harsh treatment 'as if they were not hers,' noting the masculine verb used of the hen and Jerome's quasi non sint sui; her labour is in vain, yet without distress.
Clarke (from Shaw): she neglects her little ones, found half-starved and moaning like deserted orphans.
Henry: hardness against one's own young is worst of all; her labour is lost for want of tender concern — those least in fear of losing their labour are likeliest to lose it.

outliers.note: Softens the verse's charge of cruelty into mere forgetfulness, citing Aelianus that the ostrich is in fact tender toward the young she actually hatches.

schools.summary: Clarke heaps up the ancients on the bird's stupidity (Claudian's hidden head; Heliogabalus's six hundred heads) and, with Young, praises the sacred author's economy; Wesley: God has not implanted her the instinct given other creatures.
Gill: 'deprived of wisdom' may be 'made to forget,' the bird of proverbially short memory (Leo Africanus).
Keil and Delitzsch render that Eloah caused her to forget wisdom and gave her no share of understanding.
Henry: the art of nourishing the young is God's gift, denied where it does not exist — by the ostrich's folly, as by the ant's wisdom, we learn to be wise.

themes: learning wisdom from the bird's folly

schools.summary: Clarke: her motion is composed of running and flying, using wings as sails (Xenophon: no horse could reach her); Wesley: she scorns her pursuers through sheer swiftness.
Gill: the eight-foot bird raises herself and erects her wings for running when alarmed.
Henry: careless of her eggs but fierce for her own life, she scorns the horse and rider — those least under natural affection often contend most for self-preservation.
Ellicott notes the ostrich runs in a curve (letting horsemen overtake her) and suggests the subject here is really the stork, which soaring can baffle all pursuit.

outliers.note: Reads the 'lifteth up herself... scorneth the horse' of the stork rather than the ostrich, the soaring bird baffling horsemen where the running ostrich can be overtaken in her curve.

themes: she scorns the horse and rider

schools.summary: Clarke's long note records the Guardian's critique setting the sacred poet above Homer and Virgil (the beauties flowing from an inward principle) and takes 'thunder' of the tossing mane (Bochart); Wesley: a metaphor for force and terror.
Henry sets the serviceable war-horse against the wild creatures, the flowing mane clothing his neck; strength from God, who yet delights not in it (Ps. 147:10; Ps. 33:17).
Ellicott glosses 'thunder' as terror (allowing the mane); Keil and Delitzsch render 'clothe his neck with flowing hair.'
Gill: the war-horse's strength denotes fortitude and courage, both God's gift.

debates.question: Does 'clothed his neck with thunder' mean the mane or terror?

themes: the sacred poet above Homer and Virgil

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the grasshopper of a bounding leap (the caracol) and 'snorting' of the nostrils, not neighing; Ellicott renders 'made him to leap as a locust.'
Gill offers both senses — 'make him timid as a grasshopper' or 'make him leap like one' — preferring the leaping the horse is famed for.
Clarke reports Good's 'launch forth as an arrow,' the verb uniting rapidity and coruscation.
Henry: the glory of the horse's nostrils, snorting and throwing foam, is terrible — perhaps a statelier breed than any now.

debates.question: How is the first clause to be rendered?

schools.summary: Clarke renders 'they dig in the valley,' the horse scooping sods as in Virgil's cavat tellurem; Wesley notes horse-battles were pitched in valleys.
Ellicott marks the number-shift ('they paw' plural, 'he rejoiceth' singular); Keil and Delitzsch render the bounding advance 'to meet an armed host.'
Gill: impatient in the valley where cavalry musters, he rises, paws, prances, and digs the earth.
Henry: frolicsome and proud of his strength — with more reason than the wild ass of v.8, for he uses it in man's service, not in contempt of man.

themes: the horse's obedient spirit versus the wild ass

schools.summary: Gill: he mocks at fear, unmoved by terrible arms and numerous armies.
Henry: fearless before sword, quiver, and spear, he inspires courage into his rider — and pictures the presumptuous sinner who mocks God's terrors (Jer. 8:6).
Keil and Delitzsch render 'he laugheth at fear, and turneth not back from the sword.'
Clarke preserves Coverdale: 'his stomach is not abated, neither starteth he aback for eny swerde.'

themes: the emblem of the presumptuous sinner

schools.summary: Gill weighs whether the quiver is the enemy's whizzing arrows or arrows rattling on the horse's own back (Homer, Virgil), preferring the former.
Wesley: the quiver is put for the arrows shot against horse and rider; Clarke gives Good's and Coverdale's versions of the rattling quiver and glittering spear.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the quiver rattleth over him, the glittering lance and spear.'
Henry: rattle the quiver and brandish the spear to turn him back, and he will not retreat.

themes: arms that only feed his ardour

schools.summary: Clarke (Guardian) calls 'he swalloweth the ground' the boldest image for swiftness, an Arabic idiom still current; Wesley reads 'believeth not' of the horse scarce believing his ears for gladness.
Ellicott reads 'neither believeth he' of the horse disregarding the trumpet as if disbelieving the call; Keil and Delitzsch render 'standeth not still when the trumpet soundeth.'
Gill: so eager he seems to swallow the ground rather than run upon it.
Henry: he curvets and prances with such violence he seems to swallow the ground — high mettle the praise of a horse, not a man.

debates.question: What is meant by 'neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet'?

sides.position: he disregards the trumpet, as though not believing the call has come
he can scarcely believe his ears for gladness that the call has come

themes: disbelief or gladness at the trumpet

schools.summary: Clarke hears in He'ach the very first note of the neigh, the gutturals expressive of fierce anticipation (with Coverdale's 'Tush, sayeth he'); Wesley reads the 'ha, ha' of proud, joyful neighing and 'thunder' of the captains' clamour.
Ellicott glosses 'among the trumpets' as 'as often as the trumpet soundeth'; Keil and Delitzsch render the scented battle and the shout of war.
Gill: 'ha, ha' signifies the horse's pleasure in the trumpets, uttered by neighing.
Henry: trumpet, captains, and shouting are bellows to his innate courage — how wonderfully the creatures are fitted to their designed service.

themes: he smelleth the battle afar off

schools.summary: Clarke identifies the hawk/falcon (nets, 'the wind's emblem') and expounds the southward migration whose timing no man teaches (cf. Jer. 8:7); Wesley: she flies south at winter's approach, unable to bear cold.
Henry: the hawk's swift southward flight, especially when casting her plumes, is a wisdom God gave, not man — a pity the reclaimed hawk be abused to God's dishonour.
Ellicott observes the more symmetrical order would set the ostrich between the war-horse and the hawk, a transition from the fleetest quadruped to the fleetest bird.
Gill notes the Vulgate's 'doth she grow feathered' (fledging or yearly moult), but neither flight nor feathers is owing to men.

themes: the birds as proofs of providence
the order of the divine speech

schools.summary: Gill: not at Job's command but by God-given instinct the eagle steers straight upward to the clouds (Apuleius), where other birds only circle.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'or is it at thy command that the eagle soareth aloft, and buildeth its nest on high?'
Clarke: her sight is so acute she spies a small fish while herself unseen; Wesley: she mounts out of sight, which no other bird can do.
Henry: a royal bird yet a bird of prey (whose empowering may reconcile us to oppressors' prosperity); she soars by God's instinct, not any strength from Job.
Gill: she nests on the inaccessible precipice (Pliny), the tooth of the rock like a fortified place.
Clarke: 'the crag' is shen sela, the tooth of the rock where man dares not follow; 'the strong place' (metsudah) Good reads 'ravine.'
Keil and Delitzsch render the eyrie upon 'the crag of the rock and fastness.'
Henry makes the eyrie a parable of false security: secure sinners think themselves safe as the eagle, but 'I will bring thee down thence' (Jer. 49:16).
Gill: from the high rock she spies hidden prey in valley and sea; the original says she 'diggeth' the prey, as men search for hidden treasure.
Clarke marshals Horace, Aelian, and Homer ('most quick-sighted of all fowls') on the eagle's proverbial sight; Wesley: she looks on the sun yet spies the smallest prey from beyond our sight.
Henry turns her downward gaze into an emblem of the hypocrite who, seeming to rise toward heaven, keeps eye and heart on earthly prey.

outliers.note: Allegorizes the eagle's far-seeing downward gaze as the hypocrite who, professing to rise toward heaven, keeps his eye and heart on earthly prey (a widow's house to devour).

schools.summary: Gill: the young suck up blood as the dam, the eagle drinking her prey's blood (and Aelianus so of the hawk).
Clarke: she feeds her young not carrion but newly-slain prey; 'where the slain are, there is she' our Lord quoted (Matt. 24:28), a proverb fitted to Rome's coming judgment on the Jews.
Ellicott compares Matt. 24:28 and Luke 17:37; Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet, closing their strophe on the birds of prey.

Henry: she smells the battle (in another sense than the horse, v.25); the fowls are called to the supper of the great God (Rev. 19:17); the whole gallery obliges us to confess our ignorance and glorify God.

themes: where the slain are, there is she
the gallery closed at the field of the dead
silence and worship before God's wisdom
